A Pistol in a Court-Room. MANDAN, DAK., Aug. 22.—In the District Court yesterday afternoon, while G. S. Ray and others were being tried before a jury for robbing a man in a saloon several days ago, John Coleman, a witness, was shot by Mabel Gray, one of the defendants, with a small revolver. Two bullets hit Coleman, one in each leg. Coleman had just given damaging evidence against the Gray woman. She was immediately arrested and put in jail. Coleman's injuries are not serious. Mr. Randall at Long Branch.
LONG BRANCH, Aug. 22. —Mr. Samuel J. Randall has arrived at the West End Hotel and will remain several days. He is in good health and spirits and says the action of the last House in relation to the appropriation bills is matter of record. No misrepresentations can change the truth. He has no idea that the powers of the Appropriation Committee will be in any way crippled or that any new departure will be made likely to render raids upon the Treasury easier than they now are. The Democrats will make a good fight in Pennsylvania this year, although the odds are so largely against them. Mr. Randall regards the action of the Ohio Democracy as wise, and thinks there ought to be a very good chance for Governor Hoadly's re-election.

Increase in Passenger Rates.

New York, Aug. 22.—The general passenger agents of the West Shore, Erie, Lackawanna and New York Central roads met yesterday and advanced rates to date from this morning. The following are the principal changes: To Chicago, old rate, $9.50 first class; $7, second class; new rates, $14 and $11. To St. Louis, old rates, $11.50 and $9; new rates $17.50 and $14.50. To Cincinnati, old rates, $9 and $7; new rates, $13 and $10. The above rates are for the New York Central. The Erie, West Shore and Lackawanna roads will charge the same for second class, but $1 less for first class. The Pennsylvania was not represented. Its rates to Chicago are $15 and $13. It is thought that it will conform to the new schedule.

Aufdemordte Going Home.

NEW LAREDO, MEX., Aug. 22.—Aufdemordte, the New Orleans defaulter, accompanied by Chief of Police Garcia of Monterey, Duputy U. S. Marshal Parker of New Orleans, Collector Jerome of Corpus Christi and U. S. Consul Campbell of Monterey, passed through here on the Mexican National train last evening destined for New Orleans, via Laredo, Tex. Very little money was recovered from Aufdemorte.

Failed to Deliver the Cattle.

FORT WORTH, TEX., Aug. 22.—William Hudson of Bosque County, Texas, was arrested here last evening, charged with swindling V. F. Randolph of New Jersey out of $30,000. Hudson contracted to deliver to Panolph 5,500 head of cattle, but, it is alleged, failed to deliver a single head, notwithstanding the advance payment of $30,000.

Lynch Law Sought in New York.

NEW YORK, Aug. 22.—The negro, Goode, alias Booker, who killed Policeman North last night, when taken from the Old Slip Station-House this morning to the Tombs was surrounded by a crowd who yelled "Lynch him," "Kill the black hound," etc. He was committed without bail.
goode-alias-booker-new-york-1885-08-22.A2:
MURDER OF A POLICEMAN. OFFICER NORTH STABBED IN BROADWAY BY A NEGRO.
Two Thrists of a Dirk into his Threat—Staggering Down Wall Street and Dying on the Sidewalk Opposite No. 21—Arrest of the Murderer—He Wanted to be Treated Like a White Man—The Prosecution.

James North was appointed policeman on May 6 last. His probation lasted only one month, and on June 6 he was full-fledged, and was assigned to the Old slip precinct. Lately he has been on the beat at the corner of Wall Street and Broadway. He was only 23 years old, and was married and had three children. His family lived at 421 East Nineteenth street, and he slept there when he could get off.

Last night, on the southeast corner of Wall Street and Broadway, he met Mrs. Mary Ann Masterton, a young woman, who is married and lives at 10 West street. She intended to call for Europe this morning, and she came up to have a farewell chat with North.

They were talking together when Samuel B. Booker came along. He is a surly colored man, who is assistant janitor at 20 Nassau street and sleeps in room 26. He shoved rudely past the policeman and the woman. North with his open hand pushed Booker to one side. Booker raised his fist to strike, and the policeman drew back. They struck one blow each. Then the policeman brandished his club. The negro drew a knife, and, holding it in his hand so that it would stab as a stiletto and not gash like a razor, lunged rapidly twice at the policeman. The first stroke sunk the blade of the knife in the right side of the policeman's throat, near the collar bone. The next thrust stuck the knife in higher, and above the glottis. Then the negro turned and ran up to Pine street and down Pine street toward the East River. Edward Frazell of 106 Greenwich street was the nearest man. He ran after the negro, and cried "Police!" "Police!" As the negro ran many of the district telegraph watchmen in the neighborhood heard Frazell's cry and joined the chase. Policeman Newer was at Water and Pine streets. The crowd saw him and shouted, "Collar him!" Newer collared the negro and put nippers on him.

"He's stabbed a policeman," panted the men who were chasing.

"I'd do the same thing to you. All that I want is to be treated like a white man," said the negro to his captor.

Newer took him to the station house. His name was put down on the book as S. B. Goode and his age as 42. In his pockets were found two dimes, two five-cent pieces, eighteen cents, two big different cuff buttons, three keys, an ordinary penknife and a letter from Celia Brown, care Mrs. Jackson, Quogue, Long Island. It was affectionate, and told Booker how much she wanted to get back to New York. The spelling was wretched.

While the crowd all followed the negro, Policeman North staggered down his beat on the South side of Wall street. He did it automatically and without knowing it. Frazell, before starting on the chase, asked him, "Are you hurt?" North said nothing. His girl cousin was terrified and weeping. As North swayed down the little hill to Nassau street his steps tottered and his head sank. In front of the Commercial Cable Company's door he fell. The blood, that had been pouring in a little rivulet over his clothes, gushed in a big stream over the flags and into the gutter. J. C. Wallace, who lives at 31 Bowery, tore and cut open his waistcoat and shirt and tried to stanch the blood. An ambulance was called, and before midnight it was drawn up to the curb, and policemen were getting ready the stretcher. North lay on the flags, with his head on a cushion that Wallace had brought. He was on his back, and his feet, heavy shod, hung over the curbstone. Before they could lift him into the ambulance he died.

It was just a quarter of an hour to midnight when he was stabbed. Before the clock had struck the ambulance had returned, because it was useless, and six policemen were carrying the body to the station house on a stretcher.

The knife was found. It was a snap dirk. The blade was three inches long and the handle four.

At the station house the negro made a short statement. He said he wanted to be treated like a white man, and that he stabbed the policeman because the policeman shoved him. He was the most unconcerned man in the room. The policemen crowded round him as he stood by the desk, but he was as cool as if he had struck his dirk into clay to clean the blade, instead of into a man's throat. He is a thick set, low-browed black negro, 5 feet 5½ inches high, with side whiskers and a faint moustache.

Mrs. Masterton was in the waiting room. She said that North was called away after few feet by a janitor. She stood awaiting his return, and while she was waiting the negro approached her and said something which she could not understand perfectly. She told him to go about his business, and he strutted away. He returned after walking a few paces, and as he did Policeman North left the man with whom he had been talking, and walked toward the girl. She told him that the negro had insulted her, and he ordered Booker to go about his business. Booker replied impertinently, and the policeman struck him in the face, the girl says, and shoved him along. She then took leave of the policeman, and as she walked on she passed the negro. He did not molest her this time, but as she neared Wall street she heard a cry from North, "I'm stabbed!"

She is a pretty girl, not over 23 years of age, with black hair and eyes.

Among the people who saw the stabbing were Mr. and Mrs. F. Z. Zinug, a Swiss couple, who were coming down Broadway after spending the evening at the Atlantic Garden.

"I saw the policeman raise his club," said Mrs. Zinug. "At the same time the colored man drew his knife, and before the policeman struck he lunged at him twice. The policeman staggered back."

Booker says that the policeman cuffed him twice on the ears, and hit him several times on the head and face.

The janitor at 20 Nassau street said last night that Booker was employed by him at $20 a month, and was, apparently, a quiet, peaceful man, and had never got into any trouble before.
goode-alias-booker-new-york-1885-08-22.A3:
GOODE DENIES HIS CRIME. DECLARING THAT POLICEMAN NORTH BEAT HIM WITHOUT CAUSE.
Then, he says, he Run Away, and Stabbed Nobody—Mrs. Masterson and Others Identify Him—Capt. Caffrey Blames the Officer.

The widow of James North, the policeman who was killed on Friday night on his post in Wall street, reached the Old slip station after 2 o'clock yesterday morning and lamented over his body. She is only 23 years old, and has been married four years. She has two children. The body was taken to her home at 421 East Nineteenth street, where two wax candles burned over the coffin last night.

Samuel Booker Goode, the negro who killed North, was taken to the Tombs Police Court in the rough clothes he wore when he was captured, and into Justice Power's private room. Mrs. Mary Ann Masterson, the young woman with whom North was talking just before he was stabbed; Mr. and Mrs. Francis Zingg of Galveston. Dr. Louis Emmelheinz of Las Vegas, Edward Hayck, a Roumanian; Richard F. Scully of 104 Wall street. Edwin Frazell of 106 Greenwich street. Thomas Boyle of 74 Pine street. Joseph C. Wallace of 31 Bowery, and Henry S. Percival and Solomon Lazarus of 109 Broadway were brought in as witnesses. All the foreigners among the witnesses were lodging at 63 Greenwich street. They were going to Europe, and were coming from the Atlantic Garden on Friday night when they saw the encounter between North and Goode.

Mary Ann Masterson testified that she came here from Ireland last April. The week before she left Ireland she was married to Peter Coleman, who was a soldier in the British army. He was now working as a shoemaker in Carlow. Her father made things so unpleasant for her that she left her husband and fled to this country. In New York she had been employed in Edward Coogan's family at Maiden lane and Gold street, and her husband had written to her to return to Ireland, and she had passage engaged for yesterday. Her trunks are packed at 10 West street. On Friday night, in company with a friend, she attended the concert at Battery Park. Her family had been old friends of the family of Policeman North in Ireland. She was acquainted with North's brother in Dublin. She knew his post and she went to bid him good-by and ask him if he had any message for his brother. While she was standing talking to Policeman North in Pine street, near Broadway, somebody came along and accosted North. She moved away down Pine street, as she thought their conversation might be private. Goode came across Pine street and spoke to her, saying, "The key of my room is in the door, come along," and pointed down Pine street. She stepped away from the negro, and North, who saw she was frightened, asked her what the negro had said. She told him he had insulted her, and North went up to the negro and slapped him in the face with the palm of his hand and kicked him. The negro crossed to the opposite site of the street, muttering, and North walked up to Broadway and down Broadway on his beat. She was about going home, when the negro again crossed over, brushed past her, and followed North. She stood still on the corner of Pine street and Broadway, and in a moment heard the noise of a scuffle at the Wall street corner. It was not far from midnight, but there were a good many people in the street who were coming up leisurely after the Battery concert. She heard the negro cry:

"I'll report you to the Captain."

What passed between the men on the northeast corner of Broadway and Wall street, Mrs. Masterson says, was over in a minute, and then the negro came running up Broadway and down Pine street within a few feet of her. As he came toward her he called, "You better get away." She moved back. The cry was raised.

"Stop that colored man; he has killed an officer." She ran down to see if anything serious had happened. When she reached North he was rapping for assistance. He took off his coat, waistcoat, and hat, and threw them on the sidewalk. He swooned as he attempted to walk down Wall street, and some man came along and tried to stanch the flow of blood from his neck. North staggered as far as Broad street, where he fell and died.

John H. Allen, barkeeper for P. Gearns of 107 Washington street, said that he was sitting on the doorstep of 88 Pine street at five minutes of 12, when he heard rap after rap for assistance, and a negro and a policeman came down Pine street on a run, "Murder, stop that man!" the Policeman cried. Allen tripped the negro as he passed. He fell heavily, and Allen held him until Policeman Newell, who was chasing him, came up.

Policeman Newell said that the prisoner made a show of resistance, but was subdued without much difficulty.

Mrs. Zuigg made an affidavit in which she swore that she saw a colored man striking a policeman with his hand, moving it up and down rapidly, as though stabbing, while the policeman was attempting to use his club. The negro ran, and the policeman called for help.

Dr. Louis Emmelheinz identified Goode as the man who had stabbed North. North tried to speak once or twice, but the blood in his throat nearly choked him. North said something about not knowing how it all occurred, and then he died. Edward Hayet spoke in French. He said he was a speculator, and showed a cablegram calling him to Europe immediately. He had engaged passage for yesterday, and said if he could not sail it would cost him 20,000 francs. He testified that he saw the scuffle, and saw the negro running away, but he couldn't identify Goode as the man.

The foreigners were released by the District Attorney upon the pledge that they would return to New York by Nov. 1. Mrs. Masterson was sent to the House of Detention. She is verdant looking.

Goode was committed by Justice Power for examination on Wednesday next. He was lodged in cell 42 in the Tombs. He is a single man, 35 years old, and came to this city ten years ago from Virginia. Besides being an assistant janitor at 20 Nassau street, he was cleaner-up at the Fourth National Bank at Pine and Nassau streets.

"I did not know Policeman North," he said to a reporter of The Sun yesterday afternoon. "and I spoke to no woman in Pine street on Friday night. I was walking on the north side of Pine street, above Nassau street, toward Broadway, when the policeman crossed over from the opposite side of Pine street, and, without any cause, struck me on the head with his club; then he kicked me in the left leg and struck me a hard blow in the breast. I did not know why I was being attacked by the policeman, but, as I believed he was going to keep on hitting me. I ran away."

Goode was asked how long after North's attack on him it was that he crept up and stabbed the policeman. "I didn't stab him," Goode said, and repeated again that he ran away after the policeman had struck him three times. He told the reporter that he had no knife with him.

Police Captain Caffry said to a reporter of the Sun: "North shouldn't have slapped and kicked the negro the way he did, and the negro would not have harmed him. It was startling, at that late hour to a woman who is a stranger to the questioner, and he a colored man, to have him ask her, 'Where are those keys?' or something like that question, but you and I can readily see that he was probably mistaken, and took the woman for some female employed by the janitor. Mrs. Masterson says she felt insulted at the negro's question, and told North about him. Instead of bringing the negro to the police station, as North should have done, he started in and kicked and clubbed him. The negro did the very thing you would expect him to do—use a knife or a razor. I feel very sorry for North's family, but policemen mustn't be too ready to club and kick folks, or if they do, they must, for their own personal safety, knock them out with one blow, and have no fooling about it. North was not a good policeman. We put him on Broadway, knowing that there he would least often get into difficulty. All he had to do was to try the
penceman

Three Numbers. AN ACQUITTED PRISONER TRIES TO FORCE A SALE ON THE COURT. Daniel Henry, salesman in the carpet store at No. 2279 Third avenue, desired to withdraw the charge of larceny that he had preferred against Joseph Gleason. They had been school-fellows and old acquaintances. The court would not allow him to withdraw the charge. Dan said Joe came in the store and said, "Well, Dan, don't you want to buy some books?" Joe had three volumes under his arm. He offered to sell them for $3. The reply of Dan was that he hadn't $2 to buy a pair of shoes. Joe then laid the three volumes on the counter, went to the back part of the store, and "hoted" two pieces of carpet. Finally he put a roll of carpet, twenty yards, on his shoulder and walked out. Dan let Joe walk out with it; he did not think he was going to steal it. After Joe's arrest the next day the carpet was sent back. Witness denied giving the carpet for the books in exchange. The books were left on the counter. Joe said he was hard up. He tried to sell the books and couldn't. He went in the store and swapped the books for the carpet, which could find a readier sale. A witness said he took the carpet back, and complainant said to him, "There are the books Joe gave for the carpet. There will be no charge now; it will be settled and the case squashed." Joe was acquitted.
ACTOR CHAPPELL CHARGED WITH ABDUCTING A GIRL UNDER FOURTEEN.

Charles Chappell, an actor, was arrested yesterday on the charge of abducting Minnie White, aged fourteen. The complainant was her father, an engineer. The father, daughter and Chappell, boarded at No. 117 Crosby street, with a Mrs. Saulberry.

Chappell claims to be the leading actor in "Around the World in Eighty Days."

On the 27th of June last, before she was fourteen years, it is alleged he took the child to a certain garden, filled her with beer, and afterward effected her ruin.

The girl was arrested on the 19th of this month by Officer Berkley, of the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children, who charged her with being a wayward girl, visiting houses of bad repute. Her sister also is on the town, but who tried when she learned of Minnie's to induce her to leave the life struck out for her by the actor.

Upon being arrested and brought before Justice Power, she told this story of her ruin. Officer Berkley was ordered to investigate the case, and the facts as stated were found to be true.

Chappell was held in $1,500 bail to answer by Justice Power.

Nancy's Threat.

HAS BEEN DRINKING FORTY YEARS, AND HOPES TO DRINK FOR FORTY MORE TO COME.

Jimmy O'Neil, a little fellow, came up with a big brick in his right hand, and his cap in the other. He was complainant against his mother, Nancy O'Neil.

"Kiss the book," said Justice Murray, after the lad had been sworn.

Jimmy kissed the brick he had in his hand.

"Now, Jimmy," said the Justice, "what did your mother do to you?"

"She hit me wid d' brick on d' head, and den she rubbed my nose on't."

"You didn't like your nose scoured in that way, Jimmy?"

"No, sir."

"What do you say, Nancy?"

"That boy an' his father bate me, an' locked the door an' giv' the key t' that young kid, fifteen years o' age. Think o' that, yore honor."

"You take a little, Nancy?"

"Yes, sor, for my rheumatiz,"

"How long have you been drinking?"

"Forty years, sir; and hope to drink forty more."

"Six months," said the Justice.

"I'll kill that kid when I get out," said Nancy.

Worse than Tickets-of-Leave.

LIABIE AT ANY MOMENT TO BE ARRESTED.
John Pidgeon, aged eighteen, [residing at No. 6 Renwick street, was before Justice Murray, as a "suspect." Officer O'Brien, of the Eighth Precinct said, going over his post he saw a number of loafers, and ordered them off. Coming back over his post, he saw a crowd in the distance. When he got near he saw a drunken man on the ground, and a fellow "going through" him. Standing over the drunken man, adding by his presence, was the prisoner. The thief, who had secured the pocketbook, saw the officer coming and got the start. Pidgeon did not see him until near him, and he started to escape for the river. The officer followed and the boy ran down the wharf and jumped in the Hudson. He swam around some time, and finally had to come under the dock when Officer Ryan arrested him.

Killing of Policeman North.
THE CLUB OF A HASTY POLICEMAN, AND THE KNIFE OF A NEGRO.

Two investigations are going on into the fracte which led to the death of Patrolman North, of the First Precinct, Friday night, one by Coroner Martin, the other by Police Justice Power.

It seemed at first to be a cold-blooded murder by the negro, Samuel B. Goode, but the evidence presented yesterday before the magistrate shows that the officer provoked the crime.

In the first place the officer was violating the rules of the department; he had been talking to a young woman twenty minutes, at twenty minutes to twelve o'clock at night while on patrol.

The negro, who lived in the vicinity, in passing, jocularly said that the woman might as well be with him as the officer.

North without saying a word, again violated the rules by slapping the negro in the face, then giving him a rap on the legs with his club, and another blow on the head, and made no attempt to arrest.

This was a grave violation of police rules.

The negro left, returned, and this is the worst feature in the negro, and resumed his quarrel with the policeman. This time the knife was quicker than the club, and two thrusts in the neck fatally wounded the officer.

The case was called yesterday morning, and the prisoner arraigned before Justice Power. Mr. Pundy appeared for the people and as the prisoner had no counsel Mr. Price was assigned to defend him.

Mary Ann Masterson, the young woman with whom North was in conversation when the trouble arose, was to have sailed yesterday for Ireland. She says she is a cousin of deceased, had been here but four months, and yesterday was to sail for Ireland with no intention of returning.

In taking the case before the magistrate and opening an examination there, the object was to take the testimony de ben cese to be read at the trial, but it was found that could not be done unless the accused assented.

He didn't, and after being examined, instead of sailing yesterday for Ireland, she was consigned to the House of Detention, where she may remain imprisoned a year or more.

Mary Ann Masterson (the cousin), of No. 10 West street, said she was talking to the officer at the corner of Pine street and Broadway, at twenty minutes to twelve last night (Friday). Another friend of North's came up and engaged in the conversation with the officer. She stood one side, when the colored man (the prisoner) came up and insulted her. Railroad Mechanics on Strike. MERIDIAN, Miss., Aug. 24.—Mechanics in the New Orleans and Northeastern shops in this city went on strike this morning for two months and twenty-four days' back pay and for regular pay day. There are about 300 on strike, and they seem to be stern and stubborn in their purpose. As fast as trains come in on the Alabama and Great Western, the East Tennessee, Virginia and Georgia, the Mobile and Ohio, and the New Orleans and Northeastern the strikers take the engineers off their engines and run the engines in the round house. Four trains are detained here now. Trains carrying express and mail carriers will be allowed to run, but all passenger cars will be detached. The strikers are sober and quiet. The Murdered Policeman's Funeral.
The room at 421 East Nineteenth street, the home of Policeman James North, who was killed on his post by the negro Samuel Booker Goode, was perfumed with beautiful flowers at the funeral yesterday afternoon. Two pillows of roses were the gifts of J. J. C. Connor and the Edward P. Fox Coaching Club of Nineteenth street. Hundreds of people came in from the street to look at the dead policeman's face as he lay on a bed of white satin in a black coffin. Forty Old slip policemen, under the command of Sergeant Oates, passed around the body and the weeping widow and her little son. A line of carriages followed the remains to Flatbush Cemetery.

Last of an Old Bell.

The last but one of the old fire-bell towers in this city will come down next week. Yesterday it was robbed of its big bell by a gang of riggers and safemovers. The tower stands in the rear of the house of Engine 30, at Spring and Varick streets, and was built in 1851. More than one gray-haired old man looked on yesterday who had watched at the same place thirty-four years ago, when the lookout was building. It has had three bells in its time. The one taken out yesterday was put in in time to toll for Lincoln's death. Experts say this bell's metal is uncommonly fine, and there are five tons of it. The tower is said to be 110 feet high.

Want a Say in Local Nominations.

The Irish-American Independents of the Second Assembly District, who were red hot for Blaine and Logan last fall, held a meeting in Kessler's Hall, 475 Pearl street, last night, and suggested to the Republican State Convention the nomination of Levi M. Bates for Governor and Joseph B. Carr for Lieutenant-Governor. They also said that, in spite of their labors for Blaine last fall, the Republican County Committee rather gave them the cold shoulder. They hope to be better treated this year, and to have some say about local nominations.

THE MURDERED POLICEMAN. Witnesses Describing the Death Wounds that Samuel B. Goods Inflicted.
An inquest was held yesterday in the case of Policeman James North of the First Precinct, who was stabbed by Samuel B. Goode, the colored janitor, at 20 Nassau street, on last Friday evening. The court room was crowded before the prisoner was led in between two policemen. Deputy Coroner Jenkins described the two wounds inflicted by the prisoner, one of which severed the jugular vein and caused death. Policeman William J. Newell of the First Precinct testified that the stabbing occurred near Wall street and Broadway. He saw the prisoner running toward him, followed by a howling mob, and he arrested him. The knife with which the stabbing was done was found in the area of 22 Pine street. It was covered with blood. The knife was shown to the jury. It is a black-handled jackknife, with a keen 4½-inch blade.

Policeman Robert Irwin, who was patrolling on Broad street at the time, said:

I ran to the place where Policeman North was lying. He was bleeding profusely, and evidently dying. I asked him what caused the trouble and he replied, "Nothing at all." He never spoke after that, and died in a few minutes.

Dr. Louis Emanuel Luiz of Las Vegas, New Mexico, said:

I was coming down Broadway when I saw a scuffle, and then saw the prisoner break away and run past me. I went up to the dying man, who was lying upon the sidewalk. The policeman struggled to his feet, and grasping his club, made three rups. He then sank upon the pavement again, and died in a few moments. Just before I went up to the policeman the prisoner ran past me. The electric light fell upon his features, and I recognize the prisoner here as the man.

Soloman Lazarus of 77 South Eighth street, Williamsburgh, a night watchman in Broadway, near Pine street, said:

I heard a fuss, and a cry of "Stop thief." I saw a colored man running down Pine street toward the East River, with several men in chase. I joined in the chase, and came up to the prisoner near Water street. He either fell down or sat down, and appeared to be exhausted. He said to me: "Go away; I've done nothing. He hit me first." Just then the policeman came up and arrested him.

Henry G. Percival of 194 Broadway, watchman, who was on Broadway, heard the cry of "Stop thief!" and joined in the chase, and recognized the prisoner as the man they were chasing. He continued:

When opposite 22 Pine street I saw him throw something away, and heard it strike in the areaway. It was afterward found by a boy, and proved to be the knife produced here in court.

Mary A. Masterson of 10 West street said:

At 11% P.M. I went on Broadway, near Pine street, to see Policeman North, to get any message that he wanted to send to the old country to his brother, as I intended leaving for Ireland on the next day. After I had talked with him I bid him goodby, and started down Broadway to go to my boarding house, and Policeman North turned to walk up Broadway. Just as I was about to cross the street the prisoner said to me:

"There's a key down there," pointing to an areaway; "I want you down there."

I said to him, "You had better let me alone." Just then Policeman North came up and said to the prisoner:

"What are you insulting that girl for? You have no right to do that."

He shapped the negro on the cheek and kicked him. The prisoner retreated to the opposite side of the street and in passing me said: "You had better get away from here," shaking his fist at me.

North heard the remark and came up to the prisoner, when the latter said: "I'll report you to the Captain." Immediately I saw a struggle. It was of short duration. Then the prisoner ran down Pine street and I leaved North.

I ran up to him and saw the blood gushing from his throat. I asked him what was the matter, when he said: "I am gone." He turned over on his side and died.

Richard F. Scully, janitor, said:

I was on Broadway and had just left North when I saw the prisoner come up to North and say, "You are the first officer that ever insulted me. I'll fix you." Shortly after I heard the cry of "Stop thief!" and found North dying.

Edward C. Frizell of 106 Greenwich street, a night watchman at 10 Wall street, said:

Just before the stabbing Policeman North, who was standing at Pine and Broadway, called to me to come to him. As I started I saw the prisoner rush at North and exclaim, "I'll fix you." North pushed him off, when the prisoner again rushed at him. They clinched, and I saw the prisoner make two rapid blows, and in the electric light I saw something bright flash in the light. The prisoner then broke away. I went to North, and he pointed at the fleeing prisoner, and holding his hand to his throat, tried to articulate, but could only make a gurgling sound.

The jury, after a few minutes' deliberation, brought in a verdict that the deceased policeman came to his death from a stab wound inflicted by the prisoner, Samuel B. Goode. The prisoner was committed without bail.

While He is Talking to a Young Woman a Colored Janitor Insults Her, and the Officer Resenting It is Stabbed and Dies Almost Immediately.
New York, Aug. 22.—Policeman James North, of the First precinct, was stabbed by S. Booker, the negro janitor of the building No. 20 Nassau street, at the corner of Wall and Broadway, at 11:15 last night, and died in five minutes.

North, who was appointed on the force only four months ago, was standing on the northeast corner of Wall and Broadway talking to Mary Ann Masterson, a young girl from Dublin, North's home. The girl was an old friend of the officer and was to have sailed for Ireland. While they were talking Booker approached from Pine street and accosted the girl. North ordered him to move on, to which the negro made some retort, whereupon the policeman repeated his order, emphasizing it by slapping the negro's face. At this Booker drew his knife, and plunging it into the officer's throat, turned and ran rapidly up Broadway to Pine, closely pursued by Private Watchman Edward Fitzgerald, who witnessed the stabbing. The fugitive turned down Pine, and a crowd of volunteers, attracted by the cries of "Police!" and "Murder!" followed.

At Water street he was caught by Officer Wm. J. Newell, of the First precinct. He took his arrest very coolly, simply saying:

"I am as good as a white man, and want to be protected," alluding to the presence of the crowd which had gathered. He was taken at once to Old Slip station. The officer traced up his line of flight and picked up the weapon with which he had committed the crime on Pine street, near Broadway. It is a four-inch bladed clasp dirk knife, the blade being about half an inch in width. It had recently been sharpened and had an edge like a razor.

At the station Booker was searched, and in his possession was found a letter for Cecilia Brown, of Quogue, L. I.; forty-eight cents in pennies, another knife of the corkscrew pattern, a pair of cuff buttons, a pencil and some keys.

Booker is a coal-black, powerfully built negro. of medium height and strong physique. He wears closely trimmed side whiskers and mustache. While not apparently altogether unconcerned, he seemed not to appreciate the gravity of the crime of which he was charged, and replied stolidly to questions put to him. He was just being removed to his cell, when the stretcher, on which the body of his victim was lying, was borne into the station.

Immediately after the stabbing occurred a fire alarm call was sent to Chambers Street hospital, and an ambulance, with Surgeon Horling, was sent to the scene of the tragedy. The dying officer had been assisted from Broadway to the corner of Wall and Nassau streets, it not being at first supposed that the wound was dangerous.

When at the intersection of the last-named streets the wounded policeman staggered, and would have fallen but for the support given him. Blood was pouring from the wound in his throat, and his face was ghastly pale. His clothing was saturated with blood, and a stream trickled from his body as he was led along the sidewalk, leaving a crimson trail from Broadway to Nassau street.

Dr. Horling made a hurried examination of the wound, and found it to be about one inch in width. The blade had entered just above the sternum, and the depth of the wound could not be accurately determined though the carotid artery appeared to have been severed. The man was unconscious when the ambulance arrived, and did not regain consciousness, but bled rapidly to death. The body was removed to the First precinct, where it was viewed by the coroner.

Mary Masterson, the unfortunate cause of the tragedy, stated to a reporter that she went to the corner of Wall street and Broadway to meet North by appointment, having promised to say good-by to him before sailing to Dublin. After about twenty minutes' conversation North turned to speak to a man, when the negro approached her, saying, "Good evening, miss," and making some remark about finding the key in the door. She turned to the officer and complained of having been insulted by the negro, when Booker made another insolent remark. Fearing there would be trouble between the men she turned and went towards Pine street. A moment later she heard sounds of a scuffle, and turning she saw the negro running towards her. She hastened towards North, who was feebly rapping for assistance, and found the blood gushing in torrents from the gaping wound in his throat.

For the present, the nightmare of party neutralizes all our efforts and bars the advancement of the race. The Colored Murderer. Last week a colored man killed a police man in the lower part of this city, under cir cumstances which would frequently lead to such deplorable results if it were not for the phenomenal spirit of good nature and fore bearance characteristic of the typical New Yorker. It appears that the policeman was talking to a woman on his beat. It was stated that the woman was a relative of his and had eome to bid him good bye preparatory to leaving for Europe. While the policeman’s attention was distracted from the woman for a moment, the colored man, who was employed by a down town janitor, passed the woman and made a remark to her which would seem to indicate that he mistook her for some other woman. The woman, when the policeman approached her again, told him that the colored man had insulted her. Upon this information the guardian of the public peace, instead of arresting the man, proceeded to club him. The colored man resented this, and in the scuffle that en sued, he stabbed the policeman to death. The unfortunate policeman, according to the testimony of his chief, bore a hard rep utation. In the first place, he had no busi ness to be talking to a woman while he was on duty. That is very evident. In the second place, if the man did insult the wo man it was the duty of the policeman to ar rest him and conduct him to the police sta tion. He had no right to club the man. Such things are greatly to be deplored by all good citizens; but it is not to be denied that in too many instances the police of New York assume too much and stretch their authority altogether too far. In a case of this kind there is the strongest possible evidence that the policeman was in the the wrong and that his murderer acted largely in self-defense. It is not, however, for us to sit in judg ment upon such grave matters. They can very properly be left to the courts, where we have a right to expect that justice based upon the law and the evidence will be done. It behooves colored men, no less than white ones, to refrain when possible from breaking the laws, in their letter or spirit. FOUR MURDERERS ARRAIGNED.
as T. Holland, who killed "Tom" Da
James T. Holland, who killed "Tom" Davies, the swindler, on August 31, was arraigned yesterday before Recorder Smyth in the Court of General Sessions for pleading. He pleaded not guilty in a low voice and was immediately sent back to the prisoner's pen. Samuel R. Goode, the colored man who killed Policeman North on the night of August 21, was next arraigned. District-Attorney Martine asked to have the case set down for trial on September 21, and it was done in spite of the objections of Goode's counsel. Alexander Smith and Peter Sweeney were arraigned together for the murder of John Hannon last April. Smith's case was set down for trial on Monday and Sweeney's for September 23.

Mrs. Nicholson's Washerwoman. THIS TIME SHE DID NOT SEND THE WASHER WOMAN TO HER "UNCLE." Catharine A. Bower, who did washing for Catharine Nicholson, was charged with stealing a dress and a cloak from her employer on June 17th. She walked out of the house with the cloak on her and did not return. Defendant was in the habit of working for Mrs. Nicholson and doing day's work. The things stolen, Mrs. Nicholson had seen in pawn. Defendant admitted to her she took the things to get a drink for herself and husband. Asked why she waited till the 9th before making the arrest. Complainant said defendant's husband had seventy-five dollars coming to him in June for a pension and seventy-two dollars more after promised to pay her when the pension came. Mr. Goldey asked if she got a warrant. No, she went to the station house and got an officer. Defendant had lived in the house with her five years. She often pawned articles for her, but always returned the money and ticket. The ticket shown her was in her name, Nicholson. During the last five years defendant had lived in her house. Complainant admitted making a demand for twenty-four dollars and she would not make the arrest. Mr. Goldey moved to dismiss the case, the complainant should have gone to court and obtained a warrant. The motion was granted. A Queer Mistake.
AN UNWARRANTED USE OF THE CLUB.
Gluseppe Brunette was walking along West Broadway, thoughtfully, when something was tossed against his back. He thought a dog had leaped upon him and he was about to be bit. Without considering, he wheeled suddenly round, drawing out his foot to kick, and let his leg shoot out before he saw the object. It was little Dominick Carsilla that had been thrown on the Italian, and he received the kick that was intended for a dog. That kick floored the little follow, and as he lay bawling, up came Officer Walsh and hit the Italian on the head, floored him, and then arrested him.

There seemed no occasion for the clubbing; he had not resisted, he was not fleeing from the officer. The court said that a mistake had been made, and discharged the Italian.

Complaint should be made against the officer for the unnecessary use of his club.

Wanted a Chew.

Rosana Loab and Owen Duffy were tenants in the same house. Rosana was in bed, when there came a rap at the door, and she said "Come in." Owen entered, and going up to the bed said, "I want a chew of tobacco." She said she didn't have it, and before she know where she lay she got three "raps," and next she lay on the floor like a bundle of rags.

"What do you say to that, Owen?" asked the Court.

"I don't know a hapurth about it."

"Were you drunk?"

"Don't remember."

"You don't remember knocking this woman senseless in her own house?"

"Don't know a thing about it."

The Court gave him six months on the Island to refresh his memory.

One of the Old 'Uns.

STILL AT THE BUSINESS AFTER THIRTY YEARS.

Barbara Miller and Walter Esse were arrested by Officer McAdam, of the Fifteenth Procinct, charged with lifting thirty dollars' worth of mohair serge from the store of Harrington & Goodman, No. 82 University Place, Friday afternoon. Big Mary gave her age as forty-five and residence at Greenville, N. J. She belongs to the shoplifting gang that dates back to the days of the Redigers and Mandlebaums of thirty years ago. Mary has fattened on crime, she now weighs about two hundred pounds and could not now, as in the olden time, pocket a roll of calico or silk away without increasing apparent bulk and attracting attention.

She was held to answer yesterday by Justice O'Reilly.

AUTUMN EXCURSIONS TO THE MOUNTAINS.—The Erie Railway has instituted a novelty in the way of excursions, which, no doubt, will be appreciated and taken advantage of by the public who desire to see beautiful scenery. On Wednesdays and Sundays special Autumn excursions will be run to Shoholo Glen and return, and, aside from the opportunity of exploring the wonders of this Mecca of day resorts, excursionists will have the pleasure of viewing the beautiful Autumn changes of foliage en route as they pass through the renowned and picturesque Ramapo, Wallkill, Navesink and Delaware Valleys.

WITHIN SIGHT OF THE HOSPITAL.—George Lindsay, aged sixty-three, a Scotohman, while on his way to be admitted to the Bellevue Hospital as a patient, dropped dead in the street at First avenue and Twenty-sixth street yesterday, within sight of the gates of the hospital.

MEN IN THE TOMBS CHARGED WITH HOMICIDE, AND THEIR KEEPERS IGNORANT OF THE VICTIMS—"HANGING IS PLAYED OUT"—IF A MAN WERE HUNG, WHO, WOULD RE-MEMBER THE VICTIM BUT FOR THE PAPERS REPORTING THE CASE?

The biggest fool criminal New York ever had was Jack Reynolds, who, because he said hanging was played out, was hung. The fool didn't have proper counsel to defend him, and his case was not appealed, and contrary to his expectations and experience, he was hung.

But Jack Reynolds's ringing words, "hanging is played out," are, nevertheless, near true. The effect of hanging is lost on the community, as there is no swift punishment for the crime; men have to recur to the papers for a history of the offense, to be reminded of it, have it brought back to the memory, to know who was killed, and all the surroundings. Nobody can tell if, before the particulars are published in this papers on the eve of execution, the man to expiate his crime on the gallows killed his victim by poison, by a pistol shot, a sharp bladed knife, a club, or his brutal, heavy heel.

ONLY A LUNATIC MURDERED.

Thomas Brown, and a man named Hagen, are in the Tombs on the charge of murder. Does any one really know who they killed, or anything about the case, and if they were hung to-morrow, unless the papers gave a history of the case, what would the public know what for, and why they were hung?

Well, they shot and killed a poor lunatic on Ward's Island, named James Ritche.

WHO WAS THE VICTIM?

William Carroll was committed to the Tombs for murder. Does any one remember now who he killed? The accused may, his keepers may, from frequent conversations with him, but if hung to-morrow, unless the papers told again the history of the crime, the people would have to ask each other, "Who was this victim?"

And when told that it was an old man named Gotleib Kalib, they would have to ask again, "Where was the murder?"

And yet it was at Seventy-second street, not five miles from the City Hall.

WHAT WAS HIS CRIME?

Thomas Dumpty is in the Tombs for murder. Hung to-morrow, and his case not re-stated, who could tell who his victim was?

In a few words, he killed his brother-in-law, Thomas Murphy.

THE WOMAN IN THE BAG.

If Louis Francis was led out to the gallows to-morrow, who would remember his crime except the police, the jury who rendered the verdict, and a few witnesses? The crime is forgotten, as well as the man. It was a regular Parisian tragedy, and at
morrow, who would remember his crime except the police, the jury who rendered the verdict, and a few witnesses? The crime is forgotten, as well as the man. It was a regular Parisian tragedy, and at the time was very sensational. It will be remembered when called to mind.

The man killed his wife, then put her in a bag and was walking down the dock with her to throw her into the river—as if she were a bag of straw—when he was stopped and arrested.

NOT YET TRIED, HE IS FORGOTTEN.

Who remembers James Fitzpatrick? Forgotten. He was implicated in the killing of old Gotlieb on the rocks at Seventy-second street.

MISCELLANEOUS STATE MATTERS. Iowa exhibits to the Omaha exposition will be carried by the Chicago and Northwestern at half rates. A TEN-YEAR-OLD son of Thomas Dentner, twenty-six miles south of Ainsworth, was thrown from a horse. His foot caught in a stirrup and he was dragged three-quarters of a mile and picked up dead. The Frontier Cattle company have
apolis and Omaha tracks, about one mile away. The Frontier company's ranch is in the Powder River country, where they have nearly 22,000 head of cattle ranging.

Omaha had quite a conflagration a few nights ago, the Willow Springs distillery having went up in smoke and flame. The loss is estimated in the neighborhood of $60,000.

At a recent meeting of the state reunion committee at Beatrice reports as to the prospective attendance were encouraging. Comrades are coming from all sections of the state and from Kansas. So far as can be now ascertained, there will be not less than 1,200 tents provided with a good prospect for more. There will be an abundance of water and camp supplies.

The Arion club of Lincoln and the Glee club of Omaha are to be asked to favor the reunion gathering at Beatrice with some of their vocal music.

The board of managers of the state fair have offered a badge worth $150 for the best drilled company, and another for the best drilled soldier. The Governor's Cup, which was taken by Co. F., of Juniata at the last encampment, will also be competed for, and there will be cash prizes for target practice.

If Lincoln succeeds in raising $15,000 she will get the Episcopal college building to be constructed at a cost of $30,000. Twelve thousand of the amount has been secured.

FREMONT has been endeavoring to reduce her dog population by the shotgun policy, but thus far the canine ranks have not been greatly decimated.

The Smith population is not as great as it was. One ran away from Omaha with a cool $100,000 that did not belong to him and another was hung for murder.

Hot weather is not an antidote for diphtheria. Cases are constantly reported in various portions of the state.

Last year Missouri in a great measure supplied Nebraska with apples; this year the home grown article, it is thought, will be of sufficient volume to answer all demands.

The official count gives Ord a population of 919. North Loop counts up 560.

At David City Anton Keyzer had his leg crushed by a wagon wheel to such an extent that amputation was necessary.

Miss Minnie Gilmore, of Butler county, is the owner of about 100,000 silk worms, whose product this year she estimates at about $800.

Lincoln has inaugurated the work of cleaning out its worthless curs.

It takes $9,000 a month to balance the pay roll of the Omaha postoffice.

Wayne has organized a base ball club that, after a reasonable amount of practice, is expected to be able to "get away" with any similar organization in the state.

Mr. Durfee, of Lincoln, has been in Beatrice looking over the ground with reference to prospects for a street railway.

John Gaeth, of Colfax county, took four or five hundred dollars home with him, and kept it in the house over Sunday. Monday morning when he looked for the money, it was missing, and no clue has been found to indicate what has become of it. There was no one in the house but the family, as far as known, and as the money was all right Sunday evening, it disappeared sometime during the night.

An Oakland correspondent writes: Corn is in magnificent condition and uniformly good as the crops usually are in this part of the state. The prospect is that in both quantity and quality they will be by far the best this year ever grown.

Joseph Susteuz, of Omaha, who some time ago lost two boys by drowning, is not dead, as heretofore announced, but his reason has been dethroned beyond recovery.

The insane asylum is rapidly filling with patients. Four were placed therein one day last week.

It was not Smith, the Omaha absconding dry goods merchant who was hanged at Osceola the other day, but some of his creditors wish it was that self-same individual.

Three thousand persons witnessed the execution of Millard Smith at Osceola.

Petitions are being circulated for the suppression of the widely notorious Crofts road-house, lying just outside the city limits of Omaha. It was there that a prostitute was shot dead last winter.

The correct figures of the late census gives Cuming county a population of over 10,000.

A SEVENTEEN-YEAR-OLD youth named Jones was twice arrested in Lincoln for supposed drunkenness, when it was discovered that he was insane.
The dwelling house of John Johnson, of Wisner, was struck by lightning the other night in five different places. The hinges to screen doors and a clock pendulum were melted. Members of the family were stunned, but no one was seriously injured.

Hon. T. W. TIPTON has taken his seat as receiver in the United States land office of at Bloomington.

BEATRICE has voted to fund the city's indebtedness.

CORONER OXFORD, says the West Point Progress, was notified that Richard Long, a well-known resident of the county, had been found dead in his house, about four miles southeast of town. Repairing to the scene the coroner impanelled a jury, and after the examination of several witnesses returned a verdict that the deceased came to his death from heart disease. He was found lying on the floor in a natural position, with his eyes wide open.

The crop of small grain in Cuming county will be the best in ten years.

FAIRBURY's population is in the neighborhood of $1,800.

The season for hail storms is considered about over, and the corn was never more promising at this season of the year than now.

EDWARD BOWLIN, a colored boy about twelve years old, who ran away from home at Beatrice last week, was drowned in Indian creek, near Blue Springs, while swimming with some white boys. He was a son of Rev. Thomas Bowlin and of the colored woman who is now known over the state as gradually turning white.

LINCOLN SPECIAL: Miss Sarah Ann Hadly, a lady living about three miles from the city, near Crabb's mill, was drowned yesterday and her body recovered about four o'clock after several hours search. She went out to the bank of the creek with some papers to read. As she did not return when expected the family went to look for her, but failed to find her. Search for the body was at once begun, and it was found about four o'clock. She was twenty-two years of age, and was living with her brother, Chas. Spicer, a baker. She is supposed to have slipped while perusing her paper.

Joseph Curtis, an old and respected farmer of Nemaha county, was thrown from his horse and sustained injuries which may prove fatal. One half of his body is affected with paralysis.

The Hastings base ball club crossed bats with the Omaha nine and got left. The two games in which they suffered defeat were played on Sunday, and that is why, in the opinion of their more moral friends, they were worsted.

Near Kearney, last week, D. B. Willard had two steers and one heifer killed by lightning. The cattle were in the pasture at the time. Two of them were about sixty yards from the barn and one about half a mile away. The lightning struck the heifer in the right shoulder and passed entirely through her, coming out on the tail, cutting it square off.

The negro soldier who was shot by the city marshal of Hastings, three weeks ago, is rapidly recovering, and has gone to join his regiment.

ALEX. CAMPBELL, of Cedar Rapids, Boone county, suicided by blowing his brains out. His mind was deranged, and that is the only reason assigned for the act.

The result of the census enumerators is being compiled at Lincoln, and returns will be sent to the various county clerks some time in August.

E. C. Hawks lost twenty-eight head of hogs the other day, while taking a large drove to Cedar Rapids from Allerton's ranche. It was a warm day.

BRUTALITY IN MARYLAND. WHAT ARE YOU GOING TO DO ABOUT IT?
A Colored Woman Taken from the Court Room and Brutally Beaten—Another Assaulted by a White Scamp—No Arrests—Silence of the Press—Other Matters.

BALTIMORE, Aug. 10.—Miss Hannah Lubbuck of Camden, N. J., is visiting her relatives and friends here. Mrs. A. D. Parker and daughter are visiting Newport. Mrs. E. A. Akles is paying Virginia a visit. Mr. Joseph E. Johnson of the well-known firm Johnson & Bro., on Franklin street, is convalescent. Those brothers are fine men and run a first-class house. They know how to take care of the pennies. Jas. H. Coleman of Richmond, Va., died in this city a few days ago.

The 3d inst. two cowardly white brutes at Hillsboro, Caroline Co., Md., dragged Kate Brown (colored) from the Squire's office, where she was waiting their trial for having in her own house a few days before inhumanly beaten her. The second whipping was more severe than the first. Several bystanders gave the poor woman no assistance at all, while the constable slyly slipped away to Cape May, where he can do the country much valuable service by drowning himself.

Aug. 4, at Hampstead, Miss Amanda Harris, aged 17, was assaulted by one John Brummel (white). The white ox accomplished his purpose and then threatened her life if she told on him. This ox has been reported to the authorities but has not been arrested, much less lynched, while the Eastern Shore brutes are held under slight bail for appearance to court. Here is another chance for the brainless mob at Towson to show its desire to protect mothers, daughters and home. If it is unlawful to protect the chastity of colored ladies, amalgamation is also unlawful. The papers have been so quiet about these outrages that one would think nothing had happened. Thus many outrages against us are concealed. When Cooper made his assault upon that white girl the papers immediately, in their editorials, set in judgment upon him; but upon these outrages there has not been a single editorial comment, yet the Herald is the colored man's friend. We did expect a protest from the Maryland Director, but it has nothing to say in defence of its people at all. And when we consider it is edited by a minister of the gospel who has put on its first page "Uncertain in religion," we expect nothing from it, because it is too uncertain in everything. There is in it a harangue with one Bloxom about "Convention." Editors should know that this age does not appreciate and tolerate slang, vituperation and brawls. We would expect them in rum mills and other places of ill fame, but we expect editors to use reason and culture. If an editor cannot answer articles without disrobing himself of editorial graces and honor and apparently dehroning himself of reason, it is best to let them pass.

The temperance people are holding forth every Sunday at the entrance of Druidhill Park. They seem to speak with that force which is backed by strong convictions, warm hearts and clear heads. They declare they will carry their banner worldwide, making it impossible for future generations to enter a world filled with rum hells. Some of them have ostracised that archangel, Daniel, declaring that he has moved over to the side of evil. They have the same opinion of the man that many other fair-minded people have.

The American showed great grief over the death of the savior of the country, while the Sun, Herald and other papers showed very little; but as beasts without hearts are non-susceptible of grief, those papers are excusable. The Director was one-fourth in mourning, claiming to be one-fourth Republican.

"Why was no indignation meeting over the lynching of Cooper held?" seems to be foremost in every breast, and after proper time for holding it has nearly elapsed, the people are very expressive of their wonder and dislike at such a course. It would have shown race pride and a disposition at self-protection which are right and commendable, and the custom of all civilized people everywhere. It is thought there would have been a Christian protest against the barbarous act, but as outrages upon colored persons fall below the notice of Christianity, we expected race affinity to express itself. It is not supposed that such a meeting would have been attended with many surface signs of success, but it would have been putting "the seed in the earth and the leaven in the lump"

Memorial services in honor of Gen. Grant were held Saturday morning at Music Hall, where appropriate exercises were carried out, and fitting tributes were paid to the life services of the great General and savior of the Union by Gen. Dana, Rev. F. B. Hodges and Dr. Frear. Rev. A. R. Palmer pronounced the benediction. Rev. H. G. Miller of the Church of the Covenant preached a Grant memorial sermon a week ago last Sunday morning.

Anthracite Lodge, No. 1629, G. U. O. of O. F., will picnic at Mountain Park Wednesday, the 26th inst. The first train will leave the L. & S. depot at 8:20 A. M.

Russel, son of Mrs. Mary Brown, who had his toes cut off by the caws a short time ago, died last Friday in the 6th year of his age. The funeral took place Sunday from Bethel Church. The Rev. A. R. Palmer officiated, assisted by Revs. W. A. Ely and H. G. Miller. Interment in the city cemetery. Mr. and Mrs. Mart Thompson have lost their infant daughter, aged one week. Eliza, daughter of Oliver and Emma Downey, died last Sunday in the 10th year of her age, after a long illness. She was buried Tuesday from the residence of her parents, Rev. A. R. Palmer officiating. Interment in the city cemetery.

Rev. W. A. Ely of Zion A. M. E. Church exchanged pulpits with Rev. S. Hancock of the Primitive Methodist Church, on Sheridan street. The exchange was appreciated by both congregations. Quarterly meeting will be held at Zion Church next Sunday. The Presiding Elder of the district, Rev. John Thomas of Binghamton, N. Y., will be present.

Mrs. Isaac Gould of Pittston was the guest of Mrs. K. H. Brown Sunday evening. George and Mrs. Overton of New York arrived here this morning.
